faqs.question: How should I choose project management software?
faqs.answer: Define your team’s workflow, ownership, deadlines, dependencies, documentation, and reporting needs. Test the same representative project in each candidate.

faqs.question: What should I test before switching?
faqs.answer: Test task creation, ownership, status changes, notifications, integrations, export, and the way the team handles exceptions and missed deadlines.

faqs.question: What costs should I include?
faqs.answer: Include seats, storage, automations, integrations, support, training, and the time required to maintain workflows.

faqs.question: How do I avoid overcomplicating the workflow?
faqs.answer: Start with a small set of statuses, clear owners, and a predictable review cadence. Add fields or automation only when they solve a recurring problem.

body:
Project Management for Startups: A Practical Buyer’s Guide

Startups need enough structure to coordinate priorities and deadlines without spending too much time administering the tool. Choose based on how your team plans work, whether you need docs and engineering workflows, and how the system will change as the company grows.

Transparency note: Current prices, ratings, plan limits, and product claims have not been independently verified. Check current plan terms before relying on a free tier or a particular feature.

Tools to evaluate

Linear

Evaluate Linear if product and engineering work is organized around issues, cycles, and roadmaps. Test triage, prioritization, project views, integrations, and how non-engineering teams will coordinate work.

Asana

Evaluate Asana for cross-functional tasks, owners, deadlines, dependencies, and project visibility. Confirm which views, automations, and collaboration controls are included in the current plan.

ClickUp

Evaluate ClickUp if you want tasks and documentation in a flexible workspace. Test whether the team can keep the structure understandable, and confirm current usage and feature limits.

Airtable

Evaluate Airtable for structured workflows that rely on linked records, forms, and custom views. Test data ownership, permissions, automation, and whether a database-style approach is suitable for everyday project tracking.

Trello

Evaluate Trello for a simple visual board with clear task ownership and status. Check collaboration, automation, attachments, and current free-plan limits.

Basecamp

Evaluate Basecamp if your team values a straightforward shared place for projects, discussions, and files. Test notifications, guest access, reporting, and whether its workflow matches your team’s planning needs.

How to choose as a startup

  1. Start with one team workflow and a clear project owner.
  2. Use a small set of statuses and required fields.
  3. Test handoffs, due dates, dependencies, docs, and integrations.
  4. Check export and how the system scales as roles and teams change.
  5. Compare current plan limits, seats, storage, automation, and support.

Methodology

This is a starting shortlist, not a verified ranking. Test the workflow with your team and choose the least complex tool that meets current needs while preserving a clear path to export and change later.
